first.rationale:
The two observed declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the funnel itself, and the objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, not a defensive revenue spike. memory_73 is the loudest temptation given the competitor's entry pricing, but it carries an explicit, self-limiting caveat: promotional pricing bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and was flagged as not generalizable. Matching a price attack with a mechanism already known to erode retention would convert a competitive problem into a churn problem, so I am declining it rather than spending verification budget re-litigating a memory that already tells me not to use it.

Among the constructive options, memory_31 (signup field reduction lifting first-week activation) and memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifting completion and time-to-value) are the two that map directly onto both declining metrics at once, which is why they are the ones I want the archived records for. They are also the two I am about to lean on hardest, and they are the ones most exposed to silent drift: memory_31 is 64 days old, memory_86 is 24 days old, both were consolidated summaries rather than raw records, and neither states the baseline population. If the original signup-simplification test ran on a cohort mix that no longer resembles today's inbound traffic, or if the onboarding-shortening lift was measured on self-serve accounts only, the stated "durable lift" may not transfer to the current mix, especially with a competitor actively skimming price-sensitive SMB accounts and thereby changing who is arriving at the top of the funnel. The observed declines could themselves be composition effects rather than degradation of the funnel, and the archived records are the cheapest way to tell those apart.

memory_57 (referral) and memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) are plausible but address neither declining metric; memory_91 (activation messaging) is a reasonable second choice and I keep it in reserve if verification undercuts the onboarding memories. Running at standard experiment scale with a retention-inclusive readout, not a broad rollout: the inherited evidence supports direction but not magnitude, and I want the guardrail metric on the same clock as the lift metric so an activation gain purchased against downstream value is visible before it is scaled.

final.rationale:
Both verifications came back confirmed, and the detail changes how I weight them. exp_86 is the strongest single record in the inherited set: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. It is the only direction on the board where the growth metric and the durable-value guardrail move the same way, which is exactly what the primary objective asks for. exp_31 also held up but is weaker and narrower than the consolidated summary implied: the lift is real (signup +15%, activation +9%) but qualified revenue moved only +4%, retention was slightly negative at -1%, and the record explicitly says it did not replicate outside SMB. That is a meaningful correction to memory_31's unqualified claim of a 'durable lift' and it is why I am anchoring the experiment on the shortened-onboarding mechanism rather than the field-reduction mechanism, even though both live under the same action label.

This directly addresses onboarding completion (-4%) and should pull activation (-6%) with it via time-to-value, so one slot covers both declining metrics. I am still declining promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 records strong acquisition and revenue lift alongside a material 30-day retention drop and an explicit warning not to generalize it. Answering a price attack by importing a known retention leak trades a competitive problem for a churn problem and cuts against sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Referral and enterprise sales-assist remain plausible but touch neither declining metric this week; activation_messaging (memory_91) stays my reserve if this reads flat.

Holding at standard experiment rather than broad rollout. The retention-positive result in exp_86 is encouraging but it was measured on self-serve accounts under a different traffic mix, and the competitor is actively skimming price-sensitive SMB accounts right now, which changes who is entering the funnel. Part of the observed decline may be composition rather than funnel degradation, and a broad rollout would bake that ambiguity in at scale. I will run with 30-day retention and qualified revenue on the same readout clock as completion, so any completion gain bought against downstream value is visible before it is scaled rather than after.
